Three-score were drown’d, three-score were thrown Upon the black rocks wild, And thus among them, left alone, They found one helpless child. A seaman rough, to shipwreck bred, Stood out from all the rest, And gently laid the lonely head Upon his honest breast. And travelling o’er the desert wide It was a solemn joy, To see them, ever side by side, The sailor and the boy. In famine, sickness, hunger, thirst, The two were still but one, Until the strong man droop’d the first And felt his labours done. Then to a trusty friend he spake, “Across the desert wide, O take this poor boy for my sake!” And kiss’d the child and died. Toiling along in weary plight Through heavy jungle, mire, These two came later every night To warm them at the fire. prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Kneel, Three

outputs.L1:
The wind blew fiercely, the waters raged;  
A ship was driven upon the land.  
A hundred human souls, preserved,  
Knelt down upon the sand.  

Three-score were drowned, three-score were cast  
Upon the wild, black rocks;  
And there, among them, left alone,  
They found one helpless child.  

A rugged seaman, bred to shipwreck,  
Stepped forth from all the rest,  
And gently laid the lonely head  
Upon his honest breast.  

And as they traveled o’er the desert wide,  
It was a solemn joy  
To see them, ever side by side:  
The sailor and the boy.  

Through famine, sickness, hunger, thirst,  
The two remained as one,  
Until the strong man faltered first  
And felt his labors done.  

Then to a faithful friend he spoke:  
“Across the desert wide,  
O take this poor boy for my sake!”  
He kissed the child, and died.  

Toiling onward in weary plight  
Through heavy jungle and mire,  
These two came later every night  
To warm themselves beside the fire.  

Until the captain said one day,  
“O seaman, good and kind,  
To save thyself, now come away,  
And leave the boy behind!”  

The child was slumbering near the blaze.  
“O captain, let him rest  
Until it sinks; then God’s own ways  
Shall teach us what is best.”  

They watched the whitened, ashen heap;  
They touched the child in vain.  
They did not leave him there asleep—  
He never woke again.
outputs.L2:
A fierce wind rose, the sea surged violently, and a ship was driven ashore. One hundred people who had survived fell to their knees on the sand. Sixty had been lost in the water, and another sixty had been hurled against the dark, savage rocks. Among those left behind, they discovered a single helpless child, entirely alone.

One rough sailor, hardened by shipwrecks and sea life, stepped forward from the others. With tenderness, he rested the orphaned child’s head against his true and faithful chest. As the company crossed the vast desert, it was moving to see the sailor and the boy always together, never far apart.

Through starvation, illness, hunger, and thirst, the two remained inseparable, until at last the powerful man weakened before the child did and knew his work was finished. He then spoke to a dependable companion, saying, “For my sake, carry this poor boy across the wide desert.” After kissing the child, he died.

The companion and the boy continued onward in exhaustion, struggling through thick jungle, mud, and hardship. Each night they arrived later and later at the fire where the others warmed themselves. At last, one day, the captain said, “Good and kindly sailor, save your own life now. Come away, and leave the boy behind.”

The child was sleeping beside the flames. The sailor answered, “Captain, let him rest until the fire dies down; then God’s will shall show us what is right.” They watched as the fire faded into a pale heap of ashes. They touched the child, but it was useless. They did not abandon him while he merely slept, for he never awakened again.
outputs.L3:
A violent storm rose suddenly over the sea, tearing through the darkness with wind, thunder, and crashing waves. The ship struggled against the fury of the water, but it could not survive the storm’s force. Before long, it was wrecked, leaving many of its passengers and crew dead. Among the few survivors was a small, helpless child, orphaned and alone, too young to understand the full tragedy that had taken place around him.

One of the survivors, a rough and weather-beaten seaman, found the child and took pity on him. Though the sailor was hardened by years of danger and hardship, he had a kind heart. He lifted the boy into his arms and made him his own responsibility. When the survivors began their difficult journey across the desert, the sailor kept the child close beside him, protecting him from the heat, fear, and loneliness of the harsh land.

As the days passed, the journey grew more terrible. The group suffered from famine, sickness, hunger, and thirst. Their bodies weakened, and hope became harder to hold on to. Yet the sailor never abandoned the boy. He shared what little food and water he had, carried him when he could not walk, and comforted him when he was frightened. Even as the sailor’s own strength began to fail, his devotion to the child did not weaken.

At last, the seaman knew he was dying. Too weak to continue and aware that he could no longer protect the child himself, he called upon a trusted friend among the survivors. With his final strength, he begged this friend to take care of the boy in his place. It was his last act of love and duty, and after making sure the child would not be left entirely alone, the faithful sailor died.

Later, the child too reached the end of his suffering. One evening, he lay quietly by the fire, warm and still, and slipped peacefully into death. At first, the others thought he was only sleeping. But when they looked more closely, they understood that he would never wake again. In that moment, they realized they could not leave him behind as though he were merely tired or weak. The child’s journey was over, and his helplessness, which had once called forth the sailor’s devotion, now called forth their tenderness and respect.
outputs.L4:
A violent shipwreck leaves a small group of survivors cast upon an unknown shore, exhausted, frightened, and uncertain of their fate. Among them is a helpless child, too young to understand the full horror of what has happened and too weak to endure the dangers that lie ahead without protection. The poem centers on one compassionate sailor who takes responsibility for the boy, becoming his guardian in the midst of disaster. Though the sailor himself is suffering from hunger, thirst, fatigue, and fear, he refuses to abandon the child or think only of his own survival.

As the survivors struggle onward, they are forced to cross harsh and unfamiliar landscapes. The desert brings burning heat, thirst, and exhaustion, while the jungle presents its own dangers through darkness, wild growth, and the threat of death at every step. Through all these hardships, the sailor carries, comforts, and protects the child. His actions are not driven by hope of reward, but by simple human kindness and a deep sense of duty. The poem presents him as a figure of moral courage: an ordinary man made noble by his willingness to sacrifice himself for someone weaker than he is.

Eventually, the sailor’s strength fails. Knowing that he cannot continue, he entrusts the child to others, hoping that they will carry the boy to safety. His death is quiet but deeply moving, because it comes after he has given everything he has for another life. The child, however, does not survive for long afterward. His later death adds to the poem’s sorrow and emphasizes the cruelty of suffering and loss.

Yet the poem is not only about tragedy. It also celebrates the beauty of compassion in desperate circumstances. Even though the sailor cannot ultimately save the child, his devotion gives meaning to his struggle. His kindness shines against the darkness of shipwreck, wilderness, and death. The poem suggests that human goodness remains noble even when it cannot defeat suffering, and that self-sacrifice is one of the highest expressions of humanity.
outputs.L5:
**The Kneel of Three**

At the edge of the old kingdom stood a stone circle known as **The Kneel**, a place where every ruler had once bowed before taking the crown. It was said that no one could lead with wisdom unless they first learned humility.

One winter morning, **three** travelers arrived at the circle: a soldier, a scholar, and a farmer. Each had come seeking power, believing they alone knew how to save the land. But when they stepped into the center, the stones glowed softly, and a voice whispered, “Only those who kneel for others may rise for all.”

The soldier knelt first, remembering the lives lost in battle. The scholar knelt next, realizing knowledge meant little without compassion. Finally, the farmer knelt, thinking of the fields, the hungry, and the quiet strength of ordinary people.

When the three stood again, none asked to rule alone. Instead, they chose to serve together. From that day forward, the kingdom was guided not by pride, but by shared wisdom — and the lesson of The Kneel was never forgotten.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a narrative ballad in the style of William Wordsworth about a shipwrecked sailor who rescues an orphaned child and journeys with him through hardship.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Sailor and the Child**

Upon a cliff of weathered stone,  
Where bent the grass with spray,  
An aged sailor stood alone  
At breaking of the day.  

The sea was grey, the wind was wild,  
The gull was on the wing;  
And from the deep there came a cry  
Like some forsaken thing.  

He turned him toward the troubled sound,  
And down the steep he passed,  
Where wreckage on the shingle lay,  
And foam was flying fast.  

A ship had struck the hidden reef  
Before the dawn was red;  
Her broken ribs were in the surf,  
Her sails about her spread.  

And there, half-lifted by the waves,  
Half-buried in the sand,  
A little child lay faint and cold,  
A shell within his hand.  

No father called across the sea,  
No mother stirred the shore;  
The sailor took him to his breast,  
And heard him breathe once more.  

“O little one,” the old man said,  
“Though all thy kin be gone,  
The God who marks the sparrow’s fall  
Hath left thee not alone.”  

He wrapped him in his tattered coat,  
And climbed the dripping height;  
Behind them roared the hungry sea,  
Before them broke the light.  

The child awoke at eventide,  
Beside a cottage fire;  
His eyes were large with nameless grief,  
His voice a broken lyre.  

“Where is the ship? Where is my home?  
Where doth my mother keep?”  
The sailor bowed his silver head,  
And could not choose but weep.  

“Thy home,” he said, “is where we go;  
Thy mother sleeps afar;  
Yet over thee, through cloud and night,  
There shines a steadfast star.”  

So forth they went, when spring was pale,  
By moor and mountain track;  
The sailor with his staff of oak,  
The child upon his back.  

They begged their bread at lonely farms,  
They slept beneath the thorn;  
And many a bitter wind went by,  
And many a hungry morn.  

But oft, beside a singing brook,  
When clouds had left the sky,  
The old man taught the child to name  
The birds that wandered by.  

“This lark,” he said, “though small and brown,  
Mounts higher than our care;  
And yonder lamb that leaps in joy  
Hath all the world to share.  

“The flower that opens in the cleft,  
Where no man’s foot may tread,  
Is tended by the same kind Power  
That gives the beggar bread.”  

The child would listen, still and grave,  
And watch the bright stream run;  
Then smile as if his sorrow felt  
The comfort of the sun.  

Through winter’s waste they journeyed on,  
When fields were hard with frost,  
And oft the sailor’s heart was sore  
For all the child had lost.  

One night they reached a ruined tower  
Above a leafless wood;  
The moon was thin, the snow fell fast,  
The road was deep with mud.  

The child was faint, the sailor old,  
No friendly lamp was near;  
Yet in that dark and homeless place  
He spoke no word of fear.  

He gathered sticks with trembling hands,  
He struck a spark to flame;  
And to the child, beside the fire,  
He whispered his own name.  

“I had a boy with eyes like thine,  
Who perished in the main;  
And since that hour I walked the earth  
As one who walks in rain.  

“But when I drew thee from the tide,  
And felt thy breath begin,  
It seemed the sea gave back to me  
The child it once took in.”  

Then closer to the old man’s side  
The little orphan crept;  
And while the snow possessed the hills,  
Within his arms he slept.  

At length they came, when leaves were green,  
To valleys broad and mild,  
Where apple-boughs were white with bloom  
And every hedge was wild.  

A village stood beside a stream,  
With bells that softly rang;  
And there the sailor found a roof,  
And there the blackbird sang.  

He mended nets for humble folk,  
The child learned book and plough;  
And peace, like dew upon the grass,  
Descended on them now.  

Yet sometimes, when the evening star  
Hung trembling o’er the bay,  
They climbed the hill and watched the waves  
That bore their grief away.  

The sailor, leaning on his staff,  
Would gaze with quiet eye;  
The boy would take his withered hand,  
And no man heard them sigh.  

For sorrow, like the sea, is wide,  
And dark its waters roll;  
But love can make a little boat  
And bear across the soul.  

And years went on; the child grew tall,  
The old man’s step grew slow;  
Yet still between them passed a light  
The world could never know.  

And when at last the sailor slept  
Beneath the churchyard stone,  
The man he saved stood by his grave,  
No longer all alone.  

He heard the stream, he heard the bells,  
He heard the distant sea;  
And in his heart the old voice said,  
“Be brave, for God guards thee.”  

So if you walk that quiet vale  
When dawn is on the hill,  
You may behold, beside the brook,  
A man who lingers still.  

He tends a flower upon a grave,  
He hears the waters glide,  
And blesses him who crossed the storm  
To draw him from the tide.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Victorian-style poem about survivors of a wreck crossing a desert, focusing on the bond between a rough seaman and a helpless boy.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Mariner and the Child**

Across the waste of tawny sand,  
Beneath a brazen, pitiless sky,  
There crept a wan and shipwrecked band,  
Who left the ruined coast to die.  
Behind them roared the sullen main,  
That took their mast, their chart, their bread;  
Before them rolled the desert plain,  
As silent as the sheeted dead.

Among them strode, with scar and frown,  
A seaman bred to storm and strife;  
His beard was salt, his hands were brown,  
His speech was hard as reefing-knife.  
No hymn had tamed his stubborn breast,  
No gentle hearth had claimed his name;  
The wind had rocked him into rest,  
The thunder schooled his blood to flame.

Yet at his side, with faltering feet,  
A little lad of pallid cheek  
Would strive the burning noon to meet,  
Too faint to weep, too worn to speak.  
His golden curls were clogged with sand,  
His tender lips were cracked with pain;  
He held the sailor by the hand,  
As ivy clings in wind and rain.

“Come, mate,” the rough man muttered low,  
“’Tis but another watch to keep;  
We’ve ridden worse when gales did blow,  
And green seas thundered down the deep.  
Hold fast, my lad—nay, never fear;  
I’ll bring thee through, so help me God;  
For though no mother waits me here,  
Thine shall not kiss a burial sod.”

At times the child, with dreaming eyes,  
Would murmur of a garden wall,  
Of swallows in the evening skies,  
Of someone’s voice that used to call.  
Then would the sailor turn away,  
And curse the sun with sudden wrath,  
Yet lift him when he could not stay,  
And bear him on the fiery path.

The strong men dropped; the weak men raved;  
Their tongues grew black, their glances wild;  
But still that rugged bosom saved  
One little life, one helpless child.  
He shared the last poor draught he had,  
And smiled to see the boy drink first;  
“Why, bless thy heart! Thou’rt but a lad—  
Old Jack is seasoned well for thirst.”

At night, beneath the cold strange stars,  
He made his jacket for a bed,  
And told of ships and harbour-bars,  
And lanterns shining green and red.  
He spoke of whales in northern foam,  
Of islands bright with fruits and flowers,  
Till sleep, like thoughts of English home,  
Stole softly through the midnight hours.

But when the dawn, with cruel gold,  
Smote all the east to fire again,  
The sailor’s step grew slack and old,  
His breath came short, his lips were wan.  
Still, lest the child should guess his need,  
He jested of the briny spray,  
And marked, with eyes that yearned to bleed,  
The buzzards wheeling far away.

At last they saw, through trembling air,  
A line of palms, a silver gleam;  
The boy cried out, “The water—there!”  
Then sank, half-swooning in a dream.  
The seaman heard, and bowed his head,  
As if he heard a church-bell chime;  
“Now God be praised, my little lad—  
We’ve made the port in proper time.”

He took the child upon his breast,  
And staggered toward the blessed shade;  
Then laid him where the waters pressed  
Cool kisses through the grasses laid.  
The boy awoke to life and light,  
And called his friend with eager breath;  
But Jack lay quiet in the night,  
At anchor in the arms of Death.

They buried him where palm-trees wave,  
And desert winds their vigil keep;  
No carved memorial marks his grave,  
No widow comes to kneel and weep.  
Yet oft the rescued child, grown tall,  
With tears no manhood can destroy,  
Tells how the roughest heart of all  
Broke—like a father’s—for a boy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a tragic rhyming poem with archaic diction where a sailor saves a child after a shipwreck but both suffer on a long journey.
counterfactuals.output:
Beneath a moon of ashen gleam,  
The shattered mast did groan;  
A ship lay broken in the stream,  
And all her lights were flown.  

The sailor, worn with brine and blood,  
Clung fast unto a spar;  
Around him rolled the wrathful flood,  
Above, one pitiless star.  

Then heard he, through the tempest’s wild,  
A small and drowning cry;  
He turned, and there beheld a child  
With sea-foam in her eye.  

“Hold fast, sweet lamb,” the sailor said,  
“Though death about us rave;  
So long as I may lift mine head,  
Thou shalt not have the grave.”  

He bound her to his aching breast  
With cord and tattered sail,  
And bore her through the black unrest,  
Though strength began to fail.  

For seven nights and seven days  
They drifted, gaunt and cold;  
No kindly shore, no hearth’s red blaze,  
No hand for them to hold.  

He gave the child his crust of bread,  
His last poor draught of rain;  
She slept as one already dead,  
Then woke to weep again.  

“Good sir,” quoth she, “my mother’s face  
Doth haunt me in the foam.”  
He answered, “Pray for heavenly grace;  
The sea hath stolen home.”  

His lips grew cracked, his beard grew white,  
His eyes were dim with pain;  
Yet still he watched her through the night  
And shielded her from rain.  

At length they spied a strip of land,  
A pale and distant line;  
He smiled, and raised one trembling hand—  
“God’s mercy, child, is thine.”  

But ere the shallop kissed the sand,  
His weary breath was fled;  
She held his cold and callous hand,  
And called him from the dead.  

The villagers, with lanterns pale,  
Found her beside the tide;  
She lived to tell the mournful tale—  
And wished she too had died.  

For oft, when storms in winter cried  
And gulls flew low and wild,  
She dreamed the sailor at her side  
Still bearing her, a child.  

O sea, thou keep’st thy secrets deep,  
Thy dead beneath thee lain;  
But some who live are doomed to keep  
A sorrow worse than pain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Please produce a 19th-century English ballad, with quatrains and simple rhyme, telling the story of a shipwreck, a rescued child, and a sailor’s sacrifice.
counterfactuals.output:
The wind was wild on Whitby Head,  
The moon was drowned in rain,  
When through the dark a good ship sped,  
And never came again.  

Her name was *Mary of the Mere*,  
Her sails were white as foam,  
She bore a crew of hearts sincere,  
And one small child for home.  

The captain cried, “God save us all!  
The rocks are close at hand!”  
Then loud there came the breaker’s call,  
Like thunder on the sand.  

She struck—she reeled—her timbers split,  
The sea leapt o’er her side;  
And lanterns flared, then sank from it,  
Far on the roaring tide.  

Among the waves a child did cling  
Unto a shattered spar;  
Her little voice was faint to bring  
A prayer beneath the star.  

“Mother!” she cried, “O mother dear!”  
The storm made no reply;  
But one brave sailor bent to hear,  
And marked her where she lie.  

His name was Tom of Hartlepool,  
A lad both stout and kind;  
He loosed his coat in waters cruel,  
And faced the bitter wind.  

“Hold fast, my lass,” he called aloud,  
“Hold fast, and fear not me;  
Though black the night and fierce the cloud,  
There’s mercy in the sea.”  

He bound her to a broken oar,  
He held her from the wave,  
And swam where lights upon the shore  
Shone trembling, pale, and brave.  

The boatmen heard his failing shout,  
They launched into the foam;  
They drew the weeping maiden out,  
And bore her safe to home.  

But Tom sank down beneath the tide,  
When once the child was free;  
No more he walked by hearth or bride,  
Nor sailed the northern sea.  

They laid him where the church-bells sound,  
Above the harbour wall;  
And sailors, passing by that ground,  
Still bare their heads, one all.  

And she he saved, when years had flown,  
Would come at fall of day,  
And set sweet flowers by his stone,  
And kneel awhile to pray.  

So sing the winds on Whitby Head,  
When storms across it sweep:  
“The sailor gave his life,” they said,  
“The little child to keep.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a solemn old-fashioned poem about human compassion after disaster, involving a wrecked ship, drowned passengers, a sailor, a boy, and a heartbreaking ending.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Wreck at Mournful Sound**

The storm had spent its wrath at last,  
And pale the morning broke;  
Along the sands, in splintered heaps,  
Lay beam and mast and yoke.  
The sea, that yesternight had roared  
Like judgment from on high,  
Now crept and whispered round the dead  
As though it, too, could sigh.  

There came the folk from cottage doors,  
With lanterns dim and worn;  
No bell was rung, no word was loud,  
Upon that bitter morn.  
They lifted from the pitiless foam  
The passengers who slept,  
And rough men bared their weathered heads,  
And gentle women wept.  

Among the wreck a sailor knelt,  
His face with salt was white;  
He had clung all night to a shattered spar  
Beneath the blind sea’s might.  
“Good souls,” he cried, “look not for me,  
Though cold my blood may run—  
There was a little lad aboard,  
A mother’s only son.”  

They searched beside the broken keel,  
They searched the weed-strewn bay,  
And found at length a fair-haired boy  
Where torn sea-roses lay.  
His small hands held a sailor’s scarf,  
His lips were still and mild,  
As if he dreamed of home and hearth,  
A sleeping, weary child.  

The sailor took him to his breast,  
And kissed his forehead cold;  
“I promised her,” he softly said,  
“To keep him from the fold.  
She gave him to me when the deck  
Was split with fire and wave;  
‘Save him,’ she cried, ‘and tell my boy  
His mother died most brave.’  

“I bore him up till strength was gone,  
I felt his fingers part;  
The sea was stronger than my arms,  
But not than my poor heart.”  
Then every soul upon that shore  
Knelt down in grief and prayer,  
For human love, though bruised and drowned,  
Had found its altar there.  

They laid the strangers side by side  
Beneath the churchyard stone;  
No kin had they in that far place,  
Yet none was left alone.  
The widow brought her clean white sheet,  
The child his winter flower,  
The poorest gave what poor men have—  
Their tears, their hands, their hour.  

And when the sailor, wan and spent,  
Beside the grave did stand,  
They placed the little lifeless boy  
Within his trembling hand.  
He gazed upon that quiet face,  
Then bowed his head and smiled:  
“Now tell his mother I kept watch—”  
And died beside the child.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
